title: Students Tune Out *Even With the Best Teachers* When We Don’t Do This One Thing
author: Shari Keller
summary: Keller argues that students disengage even under excellent teachers because school casts them in a passive receiver mode, listening and absorbing without doing anything with the information. Drawing on her own experience as a competitive but shallow student, and on her recent slide into passivity during an online course, she contends that relevance and action are what sustain attention. Her remedy is to get children doing before they know everything: a water-cycle-in-a-bottle experiment, small-group projects, real-world questions, public sharing of ideas and regular self-reflection. The piece is anecdotal and written partly for homeschooling parents, but its pedagogical claim is clear and concretely illustrated.
points: Being an excellent student is not the same as being an excellent learner, and grade-chasing can bypass active learning altogether.
Information that does not connect to students' lives or to something they must do is hard to attend to at any age.
Starting with a hands-on experiment, such as the water cycle in a bottle, makes the later explanation relevant and memorable.
Small-group projects built on real-world questions and shared publicly give students feedback and practice at self-correction.
Teachers should stop equating quiet with engaged and invite the messy process of active learning, with pauses for reflection.
quotes: The only thing that changed for me when I became a good student, was that I went from student mode—think passive receiver mode—to competitive mode. I skipped the all-important step—the active learner mode.
Student mode creates complacency, no matter how well-organized the lesson, or how enthusiastic the teacher. When kids sit still while the teacher does all the talking, they can easily drift off.

We don’t need to explain everything about say the water cycle to kids, test them on it, then tick a box on a chart if they get a good grade and move on to the next ‘lesson.’ That will do nothing to keep kids engaged.
Kids can see the water evaporate and form tiny water droplets on the inside top of the bottle, maybe even a tiny cloud if they’re lucky. Get them to hypothesize about why this is happening.

Get kids DOING before they have all the information. Start engaging them in active learning BEFORE they know everything. This way the information will be relevant, they will want more information to complete the hands-on activity and they will start seeking it out.
We are all more engaged when we have to put our ideas out there for feedback. And feedback is a great teacher.

It took me a long time to go from being a model student to being actively in charge of how and what I wanted to learn. When I decided to homeschool my three kids, I had to throw out almost everything I thought I knew about learning and rethink every step of how we teach ourselves.
